from pathlib import Path
from pypdf import PdfReader
p=Path('tmp/pdfs');p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA',r.metadata)
parts=[]

 t=pg.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 parts.append(f'\\n--- PAGE {i+1} ---\\n'+t)
 (p/f'page-{i+1:02}.txt').write_text(t)
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(parts))
print('\\n'.join(parts[:3]))

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
# STE counterexample for a rank-one adapter with one clipped weight.
# n=2, Qn=-2, Qp=1, s=1, b=0, alpha=1.
# W0=[[0,-1],[0,2]], B=[[1],[2]], A=[[0.5,0.5]].
# W'=[[0.5,-0.5],[1,3]]; M=[[1,1],[1,0]].
# Let X=[1,1] and dL/dY=[1,1], so G is all ones.
B=[1.,2.]
A=[.5,.5]
G=[[1.,1.],[1.,1.]]
M=[[1.,1.],[1.,0.]]
masked_A=[sum(B[o]*M[o][i]*G[o][i] for o in range(2)) for i in range(2)]
reported_A=[sum(B[o]*G[o][i] for o in range(2)) for i in range(2)]
masked_B=[sum(M[o][i]*G[o][i]*A[i] for i in range(2)) for o in range(2)]
reported_B=[sum(G[o][i]*A[i] for i in range(2)) for o in range(2)]
print('Masked STE dA:',masked_A, 'Eq. 7 / unmasked dA:',reported_A)
print('Masked STE dB:',masked_B, 'Eq. 7 / unmasked dB:',reported_B)
PY"

strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: jointly adapting and quantizing LLMs while eliminating a separate high-precision adapter branch at inference. Quantizing the merged base weights and LoRA updates provides a coherent mechanism for coupling adaptation with quantization.

The experiments cover six model configurations from 3B to 33B parameters, two bit widths, and commonsense and MMLU evaluations. Reported 3-bit improvements are substantial: LLaMA-1 33B reaches 67.4% average commonsense accuracy versus 64.3% for QLoRA* and 64.6% for QA-LoRA, approaching the 68.3% full-precision LoRA result.

The QAT-LoRA comparison provides a useful ablation of merging before quantization. Algorithm 1, the architectural diagrams, and the hyperparameter appendix help explain the approach. The paper also explicitly acknowledges that inference speedups have not been measured.
weaknesses: The backward derivation is inconsistent with the stated treatment of clipping. For G = dL/dWq and elementwise in-range mask M, the stated STE gives adapter gradients alpha B^T(M ⊙ G) and alpha(M ⊙ G)A^T. Equation 7 omits M, and the factorizations in Equations 20–21 do not generally hold with elementwise clipping. The paper must clarify whether the implementation uses these masked gradients or an additional approximation; this affects both methodological soundness and reproducibility.

The central training-memory claim lacks direct measurements for L4Q. Table 1 compares QAT with QAT-LoRA, which has a different computation graph. L4Q retains the full-precision base weights and can incur dense temporary merged weights and gradients, so reduced trainable parameter counts do not establish its actual peak memory. Matched measurements of L4Q memory and training time are needed to substantiate the efficiency contribution.

The experimental budgets are insufficiently controlled and documented. Appendix C assigns 25K versus 50K iterations to match latency without reporting measured times, while Appendix B distinguishes iterations from optimizer steps ambiguously. More seriously, L4Q at 33B uses sequence length 128 while the other configurations use 1304. This changes the training context and workload, complicating attribution of the reported gains.

The baseline evidence supports a narrower conclusion than superiority over existing quantization-aware PEFT methods generally. Uniform QLoRA* is a reasonable control for the chosen quantization format, but it does not establish superiority over original NF4 QLoRA. LoftQ is cited but neither evaluated nor substantively distinguished, leaving an important comparison unresolved.

Reproduction details remain incomplete despite the hyperparameter appendix: the manuscript supplies no L4Q implementation link and does not clearly specify target modules, evaluation prompts and software versions, random seeds, or validation-based model selection. Section 4.1 also names CommonsenseQA while Table 2 reports OBQA, leaving the evaluation description inconsistent.

Some conclusions overstate the evidence. Table 3 shows L4Q below QLoRA* on 13B 4-bit five-shot MMLU, 46.0% versus 46.9%, beyond the exception discussed in the text. Several smaller gains lack uncertainty estimates, and Table 4 does not consistently establish a benefit from positive warm-up steps over zero warm-up. The backward-pass ambiguity and missing controlled efficiency evidence are the decisive reasons important revisions are needed before a Findings recommendation.
